Potter C, Hyrich K L, Tracey A, Lunt M, Plant D, Symmons D P M, Thomson W, Worthington J, Emery P, Morgan A W, Wilson A G, Isaacs J, Barton A, BRAGGSS — Association of rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide positivity, but not carriage of shared epitope or PTPN22 susceptibility variants, with anti-tumour necrosis factor response in rheumatoid arthritis

passages.text: To determine whether rheumatoid factor (RF), anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) antibodies, or carriage of shared epitope (SE) and PTPN22 genetic susceptibility variants predict response to therapy in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) treated with anti-tumour necrosis factor (TNF) agents.

UK-wide multicentre collaborations were established to recruit a large cohort of patients treated with anti-TNF drugs for RA. Serum RF, anti-CCP antibody and SE status were determined using commercially available kits. PTPN22 R620W genotyping was performed by Sequenom MassArray. Linear regression analyses were performed to investigate the role of these four factors in predicting response to treatment by 6 months, defined as the absolute change in 28-joint Disease Activity Score (DAS28).

Of the 642 patients analysed, 46% received infliximab, 43% etanercept and 11% adalimumab. In all, 89% and 82% of patients were RF and anti-CCP positive, respectively. Patients that were RF negative had a 0.48 (95% CI 0.08 to 0.87) greater mean improvement in DAS28 compared to patients that were RF positive. A better response was also seen among patients that were anti-CCP negative. No association was demonstrated between drug response and SE or PTPN22 620W carriage.

The presence of RF or anti-CCP antibodies was associated with a reduced response to anti-TNF drugs. However, these antibodies only account for a small proportion of the variance in treatment response. It is likely that genetic factors will contribute to treatment response, but these do not include the well established RA susceptibility loci, SE and PTPN22.

Lv Qianwen, Yin Yufeng, Li Xin, Shan Guangliang, Wu Xiangni, Liang Di, Li Yongzhe, Zhang Xuan — The Status of Rheumatoid Factor and Anti-Cyclic Citrullinated Peptide Antibody Are Not Associated with the Effect of Anti-TNFα Agent Treatment in Patients with Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Meta-Analysis

passages.text: This meta-analysis was conducted to investigate whether the status of rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibody are associated with the clinical response to anti-tumor necrosis factor (TNF) alpha treatment in rheumatoid arthritis (RA).

A systemic literature review was performed using the MEDLINE, SCOPUS, Cochrane Library, ISI Web of Knowledge, and Clinical Trials Register databases, and Hayden's criteria of quality assessment for prognostic studies were used to evaluate all of the studies. The correlation between the RF and anti-CCP antibody status with the treatment effect of anti-TNFα agents was analyzed separately using the Mantel Haenszel method. A fixed-effects model was used when there was no significant heterogeneity; otherwise, a random-effects model was applied. Publication bias was assessed using Egger's linear regression and a funnel plot.

A total of 14 studies involving 5561 RA patients meeting the inclusion criteria were included. The overall analysis showed that the pooled relative risk for the predictive effects of the RF and anti-CCP antibody status on patient response to anti-TNFα agents was 0.98 (95% CI: 0.91–1.05, p = 0.54) and 0.88 (95% CI: 0.76–1.03, p = 0.11), respectively, with I2 values of 43% (p = 0.05) and 67% (p<0.01), respectively. Subgroup analyses of different anti-TNFα treatments (infliximab vs. etanercept vs. adalimumab vs. golimumab), response criteria (DAS28 vs. ACR20 vs. EULAR response), follow-up period (≥6 vs. <6 months), and ethnic group did not reveal a significant association for the status of RF and anti-CCP.
Neither the RF nor anti-CCP antibody status in RA patients is associated with a clinical response to anti-TNFα treatment.

gaps.question: Does a reproducible change in human butyrate exposure mediate improved glycaemic outcomes?
gaps.missing: Verified human intervention passages, measured metabolite exposure, medication adjustment, effect estimates and independent replication.
gaps.nextStudy: Prospectively compare matched metabolite, immune and metabolic measurements; pre-register mediation analysis and confounder adjustment.

gaps.question: Does the intestinal Treg change explain a metabolic outcome in humans?
gaps.missing: Matched human tissue, cell-state assays, metabolite measurements and longitudinal metabolic outcomes in the same study.
gaps.nextStudy: Measure tissue-specific regulatory-cell states and insulin sensitivity together; compare cell composition and activation state rather than inferring function from counts.

gaps.question: Which macrophage mechanisms transfer across intestinal and adipose tissues?
gaps.missing: Direct cross-tissue evidence; tissue-specific states and interventions cannot be merged.
gaps.nextStudy: Paired tissue profiling and perturbation studies with explicit tissue controls and reproducible cell-state definitions.

gaps.question: Which metabolite-associated effects in NOD mice replicate in human islet autoimmunity?
gaps.missing: Human islet-specific immunity, autoantibody stage, C-peptide, age and longitudinal progression with measured exposures.
gaps.nextStudy: Separate prevention, recent-onset and longstanding disease cohorts; preserve antigen specificity and beta-cell outcomes.

gaps.question: When do SCFAs promote versus inhibit Th17-related responses?
gaps.missing: Comparable dose, cytokine milieu, assay, tissue, species and timepoint; promotion and inhibition are not interchangeable.
gaps.nextStudy: Pre-register a perturbation matrix across dose and cytokine context with regulatory and effector readouts.

gaps.question: Can neuroimmune modulation explain a metabolic outcome in the same human cohort?
gaps.missing: Direct metabolic outcomes and source-matched human circuit evidence; an RA vagus pilot is not diabetes efficacy evidence.
gaps.nextStudy: Evaluate matched autonomic, inflammatory and metabolic measures; keep circuit plausibility separate from clinical intervention effects.

gaps.question: Which mechanisms are shared, and which depend on islet autoimmunity rather than insulin resistance?
gaps.missing: Disease stage and antigen-specific immune context. The two diagnoses are not interchangeable evidence populations.
gaps.nextStudy: Stratify by diagnosis, autoantibody status, residual beta-cell function, medication and insulin-sensitivity measures.

gaps.question: Which study criteria can be assessed for a clearly defined research cohort?
gaps.missing: Current registry snapshot, full criteria, recruitment dates, geography, medication, autoantibody and C-peptide requirements.
gaps.nextStudy: Import public registry records and inspect condition and age overlap; leave unparsed criteria and eligibility unresolved.

gaps.question: Which antigen-specific immune-cell changes explain beta-cell injury in the population being studied?
gaps.missing: Source-verified islet-specific human immune evidence, antigen specificity, tissue and disease stage. Peripheral immune-cell counts alone cannot establish islet injury.
gaps.nextStudy: Pair stage-specific immune assays with beta-cell function measurements and independent source review; separate autoreactivity from general inflammation.

questions.title: Gut metabolites → immune signalling → type 2 diabetes
questions.summary: Mouse butyrate/Treg mechanisms, human microbiome associations and human dietary interventions answer different questions. No single path establishes that gut-driven immune activity causes a person’s insulin resistance.
questions.prediction: A pre-specified metabolite–immune signature tracks a metabolic outcome after adjustment for medication, diet and adiposity.
questions.falsifier: The association disappears after adjustment, fails independent replication or lacks the predicted immune change.
questions.experiment: Prospective repeated metabolomics, tissue-aware immune profiling and metabolic outcomes, with a pre-registered causal model.

questions.title: Gut metabolites → islet autoimmunity → type 1 diabetes
questions.summary: A protective mouse intervention and human longitudinal microbiome associations do not establish human prevention. Islet autoimmunity and beta-cell function must remain distinct from insulin resistance.
questions.prediction: A source-verified metabolite signature precedes a specified change in islet-specific immunity within a defined disease stage.
questions.falsifier: Temporal ordering is absent or the immune and beta-cell outcomes do not change as predicted.
questions.experiment: Stage-stratified human observational validation before any intervention proposal, preserving autoantibody and C-peptide context.

questions.title: SCFAs, Treg/Th17 cells and inflammatory disease
questions.summary: Regulatory, effector and barrier findings depend on species, tissue, dose and cytokine setting. Mouse colitis does not automatically establish a human Crohn’s disease mechanism.
questions.prediction: Dose and cytokine setting explain a reproducible direction change in the selected immune readout.
questions.falsifier: The direction change fails under matched conditions or tracks cell viability rather than differentiation.
questions.experiment: A controlled perturbation matrix with appropriate cellular and tissue models, followed by independent human validation.

questions.title: Neuroimmune signalling and metabolic inflammation
questions.summary: Neural anti-inflammatory model findings and small human inflammatory-disease studies support questions for investigation, not a demonstrated diabetes treatment.
questions.prediction: A pre-specified autonomic change precedes matched inflammatory and metabolic changes in the same cohort.
questions.falsifier: The metabolic association is absent, non-replicable or explained by medication and activity.
questions.experiment: Prospective multimodal observational validation before a separately governed intervention study.

futureResearch.title: Living evidence retrieval
futureResearch.capability: Hybrid keyword, semantic and graph retrieval with source versions, correction checks and study-context extraction.
futureResearch.evaluation: Compare against independently labelled relevant and contradictory passages; measure retrieval recall and citation entailment.

futureResearch.title: Context-aware contradiction analysis
futureResearch.capability: Use models to propose differences in species, tissue, dose and assay that might explain apparently opposing findings.
futureResearch.evaluation: Blind expert adjudication of genuine contradictions versus context differences; report both precision and recall.

futureResearch.title: Multimodal discovery
futureResearch.capability: Combine approved metabolomics, single-cell/spatial immune profiles and longitudinal metabolic measurements in authorised research cohorts.
futureResearch.evaluation: Pre-register endpoints, batch controls, subgroup evaluation and external replication; do not treat correlation as mediation.

futureResearch.title: Perturbation and organoid experiments
futureResearch.capability: Prioritise falsifiable metabolite–cell hypotheses for gut organoid, immune co-culture or microphysiological experiments.
futureResearch.evaluation: Independent wet-lab replication, dose and viability controls, and clear model-to-human translation limits.

futureResearch.title: Privacy-preserving cohort research
futureResearch.capability: Evaluate federated queries over partner-owned cohorts with consent, small-cell suppression and access controls; no shared patient database.
futureResearch.evaluation: Privacy threat modelling, access-control tests and approved prospective protocols before any real-data use.
